summary: This paper introduces CDAS, a method combining Distributed Interchange Intervention (DII) from causal interpretability with a Jensen-Shannon divergence distribution-matching objective for bi-directional LLM steering. The core motivation — that faithfully identifying internal concept features is preferable to imposing external preferences — is sound and timely. However, the empirical case for CDAS is mixed: it does not consistently outperform existing methods on AXBENCH, requires factor tuning that undercuts its principled appeal, and key evaluations rely on small samples and inconsistent significance reporting. The paper's honest acknowledgement of limitations and its safety-focused case studies are genuine strengths, but additional baselines, rigorous significance testing, and broader model coverage are needed before a clear accept recommendation is warranted.
strengths: The JSD-based distribution-matching objective is a principled and well-motivated departure from likelihood maximization and preference optimization; the self-supervised 'teacher signal' from the model's own counterfactual distribution is conceptually attractive and clearly distinguished from prior work.

The paper is unusually candid: it states where CDAS underperforms, acknowledges that factor tuning undermines the tuning-free appeal in general steering, and scopes claims carefully throughout the conclusion, which materially raises the trust in the positive results reported.

The safety case studies — refusal override and CoT-based backdoor neutralization — are well-motivated, use multiple model families (including 70B), and the faithfulness evaluation via benchmark accuracy deltas and KL divergence provides a credible lens on utility preservation that competing papers often omit.

Framing steering as a problem linked to mechanistic interpretability rather than parameter-efficient fine-tuning is a useful conceptual contribution that should interest both the steering and interpretability communities at ICLR.

key_concerns.issue: Table 1 and the fair-score aggregation lack variance or standard-error reporting for all methods except where noted from prior papers. 'Fair scores are averaged across ten random splits' is mentioned but no spread statistic is reported, making it impossible to assess whether observed score differences are statistically real versus noise.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report standard errors (or 95% CIs) for all entries in Table 1, at minimum for CDAS and the strongest baselines. A simple table footnote with per-method standard deviations across splits would suffice and is standard practice in AXBENCH-style evaluations.

key_concerns.issue: AXBENCH evaluation covers only two model families (Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B), which is insufficient to claim that CDAS is a viable general-purpose steering method. All four rows in Table 1 come from the same model family, so the results could reflect Gemma-2-specific properties of representation geometry rather than a general advantage of the JSD objective.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Evaluate on at least one additional model family (e.g., Llama-3 or Mistral) on AXBENCH. Even partial results on a third family would substantially strengthen the generality claim.

key_concerns.issue: The practical advantage of the 'unit factor' setting (no tuning required) collapses for general-purpose steering: the paper concedes that 'inference-time factor tuning is paramount' and Table 1 shows a large oracle–fair gap. This conflates two claims — a principled objective and a tuning-free deployment — that do not simultaneously hold in the general case, weakening the paper's central contribution.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Clearly delineate the conditions under which unit-factor CDAS is competitive (safety case studies) from conditions where it is not (AXBENCH), and consider whether a method that still requires β-tuning via grid search offers a materially different operational profile than RePS with its factor grid search.

key_concerns.issue: The backdoor model in Case Study 2 is trained by the authors themselves, introducing potential circularity: training data choices, CoT format, and trigger design could inadvertently make the chosen intervention layer or DII protocol unusually effective. No external backdoor benchmark is used to corroborate the results.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Evaluate on at least one published backdoor model from the literature to demonstrate that the advantage is not artefactual to the authors' own training setup.

key_concerns.issue: The ablation comparing CDAS versus 'DAS' (CDAS with Lang. objective) — arguably the most critical ablation that isolates the JSD objective from the DII intervention protocol — is introduced only in Section 5 and not included in Table 1. It is therefore unclear how much of the AXBENCH performance gap (or lack thereof) is attributable to the objective versus the DII protocol.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include the DAS (DII + Lang.) baseline in Table 1 for the full AXBENCH comparison so that the contribution of each component can be assessed independently.

key_concerns.issue: The 'one-to-many' DII protocol selects a single source token from <model> tokens via grid search, introducing a hyperparameter whose sensitivity is not characterized; Figure 2 is referenced for this but its caption is absent from the manuscript body as reviewed.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report a sensitivity analysis over the choice of source token position, or at minimum report variance across positions in the case studies.

key_concerns.issue: Table 2 for Llama-3.1-70B appears truncated in the submitted text (suppression score and harmonic mean are missing), making it impossible to fully evaluate the 70B results for Case Study 1.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Verify that all table entries are present and legible in the final submission PDF.

questions_for_authors: Why was the 'DAS' (DII + Lang.) ablation baseline excluded from Table 1? Including it is essential to disentangle the contribution of the JSD objective from the DII protocol on the AXBENCH benchmark.

The AXBENCH training set augmentation uses GPT-4o-mini to generate neutral responses (yi) and modified instructions (xci). How sensitive are results to the quality of this augmentation, and was any quality filtering applied? Could noisy augmented data explain the large unit-factor/tuned-factor gap?

In Case Study 1, it is claimed that RePS shows 'evidence of overfitting on training labels' (H.6), but this evidence is in the appendix. Could you summarize what form this evidence takes — is it a train/test performance gap, and how large is it?

For the backdoor experiment, the n=100 training set was curated through red-teaming, 7 instructions were hand-crafted and the rest augmented with GPT-4.1-mini. How diverse is this set relative to the true trigger, and does CDAS performance degrade gracefully as the red-teaming instructions deviate further from the trigger distribution?

Table 4 reports tinyBenchmarks with exactly 100 instances each. The accuracy delta for CDAS on tinyMMLU is +2.63%, suggesting the intervention improves accuracy — is this statistically significant or within Monte Carlo noise given the tiny sample size, and was this result robust across the three seeds?
calibration_check: Claims are generally well-scoped and hedged — the conclusion explicitly delineates when CDAS is and is not preferable — but the framing of AXBENCH results as 'CDAS advances the performance frontier on Gemma-2-9B' slightly overstates a single-layer win on a single model family where RePS still outperforms at the deeper layer.

significance.justification: Principled bi-directional steering with utility preservation is an important problem, and the safety case studies are practically relevant, but the AXBENCH results do not establish CDAS as a clear advance over existing methods in the general-purpose setting, limiting the community impact.

novelty.justification: DII is directly imported from Geiger et al. (2024), JSD-based distribution matching is a well-known technique (GANs, knowledge distillation), and the contribution is their combination applied to steering; the application context is new but the core technical contribution is incremental.

rigor.justification: The method derivation is internally consistent and the JSD objective is appropriately motivated, but the empirical support is mixed — CDAS does not win consistently and the critical DII-vs-objective ablation is missing from the primary benchmark table.

statistical_soundness.justification: Table 1 reports point estimates without variance for most methods despite known result variability across seeds; tinyBenchmark evaluations use 100 instances per benchmark making accuracy deltas unreliable; only Figure 1 shows standard errors, which is insufficient coverage.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper is notably candid about failure modes — explicitly stating where CDAS underperforms, acknowledging that factor tuning is necessary in the general case, and hedging AXBENCH conclusions carefully — a genuine strength relative to most steering papers.

clarity.justification: The method section is reasonably precise and the notation is consistent, but the reuse of the 'DAS' acronym for a distinct Lang.-objective baseline is confusing, and key hyperparameter choices (β range, token position grid search) are deferred to appendices without summary.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows standard conference structure with a clear method–experiments–conclusion arc; the split between benchmark (Section 4) and case studies (Section 5) is logical, and the length appears appropriate for an ICLR submission.

reproducibility.justification: Formulas, data curation procedures, and benchmark protocols are described, but GPT-4o-mini-based augmentation introduces non-determinism, several hyperparameters (β grid, layer grid) are resolved in appendices, and the self-trained backdoor model requires replication of a non-trivial fine-tuning procedure.

related_work.justification: Coverage of steering vectors, DAS/causal abstraction, and distribution matching is solid and current, but the paper omits comparison to representation engineering methods (Zou et al. 2023a is cited but not benchmarked against in case studies) and recent activation-patching approaches.

figure_quality.justification: From captions, Figure 1's per-layer ASR plots with standard-error shading are appropriate and informative for the main case-study claim; the tables are well-structured but lack variance columns, and Figure 2 (the one-to-many DII diagram) is referenced but its caption is absent, limiting assessment.

breadth_generality.justification: AXBENCH evaluation is limited to a single model family (Gemma-2) with two sizes; safety case studies cover only two specific scenarios and are evaluated on models from one provider; the critical DII-vs-objective ablation is absent from the primary benchmark, making it impossible to assess which component drives results.

overall_recommendation.justification: An interesting and honest paper with a principled motivation, but the mixed AXBENCH results, absence of key ablations in the primary table, lack of variance reporting, and single-family model coverage fall short of the bar for a clear ICLR accept; substantial additional experiments are needed.
